title: Closures Capture Variable Bindings, Not Snapshots
description: Contrast a closure that reads a reassigned variable with a default argument evaluated at definition time, and see two closures share one mutable cell.
source: draft: agy free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Lines 3-6 define `x = 10` and `get_x()` returning `x`. Calling `get_x()` on line 8 returns `10`. After line 10 reassigns `x = 99`, calling `get_x()` again on line 11 returns `99`. `get_x` looks up the binding `x` in its enclosing scope each time it runs.

Line 14 defines `def get_x_snapshot(val=x):` while `x` is `99`. Python evaluates default argument expressions once when `def` executes, binding `val`'s default to `99` even after line 17 sets `x = 42`.

Compare `get_x()` on lines 5-6 with `get_x_snapshot(val=x)` on lines 14-15. `get_x()` resolves `x` in the enclosing scope when called. `get_x_snapshot()` returns its local parameter `val`, whose default value was evaluated at line 14.
`make_counter()` creates a one-element list `count = [0]` and returns two inner closures (`increment` and `reset`) that both read and mutate `count[0]`.

steps.question: On lines 30-33, `inc, rst = make_counter()` calls `inc()` three times (`1 2 3`), calls `rst()`, and then calls `inc()` on line 33. What does line 33 print?
steps.answer: Line 33 prints `1`, because `rst()` set the shared `count[0]` cell back to `0` on line 27 and `inc()` incremented that same cell to `1`.

steps.description: Lines 30-33 call `inc()` three times, reset the shared `count[0]` via `rst()`, and call `inc()` once more to print `1`.
At trace step 32 inside `rst()`, line 27 sets `count[0] = 0` in the frame shared with `inc`.
